name: Choosing a suitable informal unit for a measurement task
description: Students select an appropriate informal unit for a given measurement attribute, explaining why their choice suits the object being measured.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked to measure the length of a pencil, the student chooses paper clips rather than footsteps, saying paper clips are smaller and will give a more accurate measure.
commonError: Student selects any available unit without considering whether its size suits the object, e.g. using footsteps to measure a pencil.
checkpointTask: I want to measure the length of this book and the length of the classroom. What unit would you choose for each? Why?

name: Measuring length using uniform informal units end-to-end
description: Students measure the length of objects by placing identical informal units end-to-end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the total.
exampleOfSuccess: The student lines up 9 blocks end-to-end along a pencil case with no gaps, counts carefully, and records the length as 9 blocks.
commonError: Student leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, producing an inaccurate count, without noticing the error.
checkpointTask: Measure the length of your desk using cubes. Make sure there are no gaps. How many cubes long is it?

name: Measuring and comparing capacity using informal units
description: Students measure the capacity of containers by filling with a consistent informal unit (e.g. a cup or spoon) and compare two or more containers by their counts.
exampleOfSuccess: The student fills Container A with 6 cups of sand and Container B with 9 cups, then says Container B holds more because it needed more cups.
commonError: Student compares containers by visual appearance (taller looks like more) without measuring, or uses different sized scoops for each container.
checkpointTask: Fill this jar with spoonfuls of rice. Count as you go. Then fill this other jar. Which holds more?

name: Measuring and comparing mass using balance scales
description: Students use balance scales and informal units (e.g. blocks or marbles) to measure and compare the mass of objects, recording results.
exampleOfSuccess: The student places an apple on one side of a balance scale, adds blocks to the other side until balanced, counts 14 blocks, and records the apple as 14 blocks mass.
commonError: Student tips the balance and declares which side is heavier without using units to quantify the difference.
checkpointTask: Use the balance scale and these blocks to find the mass of this rock. How many blocks does it balance with?

name: Recognising that unit size affects the count
description: Students demonstrate that measuring the same object with a larger unit gives a smaller count and a smaller unit gives a larger count, explaining the inverse relationship.
exampleOfSuccess: The student measures a book as 8 large blocks long and 15 small blocks long, then explains that the small blocks give a bigger number because each one covers less space.
commonError: Student thinks a bigger number always means a longer object, not understanding that the count depends on unit size.
checkpointTask: Measure this same pencil with the big blocks and then with the small blocks. Why are the numbers different?
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M3M01 (metric units) as the inverse relationship between unit size and count is the conceptual foundation for understanding why we use standard units.

name: Ordering three or more objects by measurement
description: Students measure three or more objects using the same informal unit and order them from smallest to largest, justifying their order using counts.
exampleOfSuccess: The student measures three pencils as 6, 9 and 7 blocks respectively, then orders them correctly: red (6), green (7), blue (9) from shortest to longest.
commonError: Student orders by visual comparison after measuring, ignoring the recorded counts when they conflict with appearance.
checkpointTask: Measure these three objects with paper clips. Put them in order from shortest to longest using your measurements.

name: Recording and communicating measurement results
description: Students record measurements clearly using number and unit, and communicate results to others in a way that allows comparison without seeing the original objects.
exampleOfSuccess: The student records the table as 23 cubes long and the chair as 14 cubes long, then tells a classmate the table is longer because 23 is more than 14.
commonError: Student records only the number without the unit, making it impossible to compare results measured with different units.
checkpointTask: Measure two things in the room. Write your results so that someone in another class could compare them without coming to see the objects.

name: Identifying halves and quarters in everyday measurement contexts
description: Students recognise and name halves and quarters in familiar measurement situations such as half a cup, quarter of a metre, or half an hour.
exampleOfSuccess: The student points to the half-cup mark on a measuring jug and says that is half a cup, and identifies the quarter-hour mark on a clock face.
commonError: Student can name halves and quarters in food contexts but does not recognise the same fractions applied to length, capacity or time.
checkpointTask: Find something in the room that shows a half or a quarter. Explain how you know it is a half or a quarter.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2N03 (fractions) as measurement contexts apply the same half/quarter/eighth concepts.

name: Demonstrating halves and quarters through folding and cutting
description: Students create halves, quarters and eighths by folding or cutting objects, verifying that each part is equal.
exampleOfSuccess: The student folds a strip of paper in half, then in half again to make quarters, checking each section is the same size by overlapping.
commonError: Student folds unevenly, creating parts of different sizes, then names them as halves or quarters without checking equality.
checkpointTask: Fold this strip of paper to show quarters. How do you know each part is the same size?

name: Using half and quarter in cooking and capacity measurement
description: Students interpret and use half and quarter measures in practical cooking or capacity contexts, applying the concept to measuring jugs and spoons.
exampleOfSuccess: When a recipe says half a cup of flour, the student fills the cup to the halfway mark and explains that means exactly two of those would fill the whole cup.
commonError: Student fills to an approximate level without checking the halfway mark, treating half as roughly less than a full amount.
checkpointTask: The recipe needs a quarter cup of sugar. Show me how you would measure that exactly.

name: Connecting half and quarter to clock time
description: Students identify half-past and quarter-past/quarter-to times on an analog clock, connecting the fraction of the clock face to the duration of time.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says half-past 3 means the minute hand has gone halfway around the clock, which is 30 minutes, and points to the 6.
commonError: Student can read half-past by rote (hand on 6) but cannot explain the connection to half of the clock face or 30 minutes.
checkpointTask: Show me half-past 7 on the clock. Why is it called half-past?
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2M04 (reading analog clock) as half and quarter past are the same fractions applied to the clock face.

name: Identifying halves and quarters in length and distance
description: Students apply half and quarter concepts to lengths, identifying the halfway point of a line or distance and using language like half a metre.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a 1 metre length of string, the student folds it to find the halfway point and labels it half a metre, then folds again to find a quarter metre.
commonError: Student estimates the halfway point visually without folding or measuring, often placing the mark well off centre.
checkpointTask: Here is a 1 metre strip of paper. Find the halfway mark. Now find the quarter mark.

name: Using eighths in measurement contexts
description: Students extend halving to create eighths, recognising that eighths are smaller than quarters, and apply this in simple measurement situations.
exampleOfSuccess: The student folds a strip into eighths by halving three times, counts 8 equal parts, and says each part is an eighth and two eighths make a quarter.
commonError: Student can fold into eighths mechanically but describes each part as a small piece rather than connecting it to the fraction name or its relationship to quarters.
checkpointTask: Fold this strip in half, then in half again, then once more. How many parts do you have? What is each part called?
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2N03 (halves, quarters, eighths through repeated halving) as this IC applies that concept in a measurement context.

name: Comparing and ordering fractional measures
description: Students compare two or more fractional measurements (e.g. half a cup vs a quarter cup) and order them from smallest to largest, justifying their reasoning.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says a quarter cup is smaller than a half cup because a quarter is one of four equal parts and a half is one of only two equal parts, so the parts are bigger when there are fewer of them.
commonError: Student compares fractional measures by appearance of the quantity rather than reasoning about the fraction, saying the half looks like more without explaining why.
checkpointTask: Which is more - a half cup or a quarter cup? How do you know without filling them up?

name: Reading and navigating a calendar
description: Students identify specific dates, days of the week, and months on a calendar, using correct terminology.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a calendar for May, the student can find the 15th, name the day it falls on, and identify how many Tuesdays are in the month.
commonError: Student confuses rows (weeks) with columns (days), misreading the calendar grid structure.
checkpointTask: Look at this calendar. What day is the 20th? How many Fridays are in this month?

name: Locating specific dates and identifying the day of the week
description: Students use a calendar to find a given date and name the corresponding day, and conversely, find dates for a given day.
exampleOfSuccess: The student uses the June calendar to find that the 12th is a Wednesday, and that the next Friday after June 5 is June 7.
commonError: Student counts calendar squares from the start of the month each time rather than reading across from the day heading.
checkpointTask: What day of the week is June 23? What is the date of the first Monday in June?

name: Counting days between two dates using a calendar
description: Students count the number of days between two given dates on the same calendar month, using the calendar grid to count accurately.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked how many days from June 8 to June 15, the student counts the squares from 9 to 15 and answers 7 days, not counting the start date.
commonError: Student includes the start date in the count, giving an answer one more than the correct number of days.
checkpointTask: How many days is it from the 3rd to the 17th of this month? Show me how you counted.

name: Finding dates a given number of days forward or backward
description: Students use a calendar to find the date that is a given number of days before or after a stated date, crossing week boundaries.
exampleOfSuccess: Starting from June 10, the student counts forward 14 days on the calendar and correctly lands on June 24.
commonError: Student adds the number directly to the date (10+14=24) without using the calendar, which only works when the result stays in the same month.
checkpointTask: Today is the 5th. The excursion is in 12 days. What date is the excursion?
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2N06 (mathematical modelling with calendars) as this IC directly supports modelling how many days are left in the year.

name: Counting days between dates across month boundaries
description: Students determine the number of days between two dates that span a month boundary, combining days remaining in one month with days into the next.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked how many days from June 25 to July 8, the student counts 5 days left in June plus 8 days in July to get 13 days total.
commonError: Student tries to subtract the dates directly (25-8) without accounting for the month boundary and remaining days.
checkpointTask: How many days from the 28th of this month to the 10th of next month? Show your working.

name: Creating and using a class calendar for planning
description: Students create or annotate a class calendar by entering specific dates and events, then use it to answer questions about timing and sequence.
exampleOfSuccess: The student enters the sports carnival (June 14), the library visit (June 21) and the last day of term (June 27) on a blank calendar, then correctly identifies that the library visit is one week before the last day.
commonError: Student enters dates correctly but cannot use the completed calendar to answer comparative questions without recounting from scratch.
checkpointTask: Add these three events to your calendar. Which comes first? How many days between the first and last event?

name: Identifying the hour and minute hands on an analog clock
description: Students correctly name and distinguish the hour and minute hands, explaining the role of each in showing the time.
exampleOfSuccess: The student points to the short hand and says that is the hour hand and it shows which hour we are in, and points to the long hand and says that is the minute hand and it shows the minutes.
commonError: Student confuses the two hands, often thinking the longer hand shows hours because longer means more.
checkpointTask: Point to the hour hand. Point to the minute hand. What does each one tell us?

name: Reading and showing time to the hour
description: Students read times shown on the hour on an analog clock and set a clock to a given hour time.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown a clock with hands at 12 and 3, the student says 3 o clock. When asked to show 7 o clock, the student places the minute hand on 12 and the hour hand on 7.
commonError: Student reads the number the minute hand points to as the hour, e.g. reading 3 o clock as 12 o clock when the minute hand is on 12.
checkpointTask: What time does this clock show? Now show me 9 o clock on the clock.

name: Reading and showing time to the half-hour
description: Students read and show half-past times, connecting the position of the minute hand on 6 to half of the clock face being completed.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown half-past 4, the student says the minute hand is on 6 which means half the clock face has gone around - that is 30 minutes - so it is half-past 4.
commonError: Student reads the hour hand position without noticing it has moved past the hour, reading half-past 4 as 4 o clock or 5 o clock.
checkpointTask: What time is this? Show me half-past 11 on the clock.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2M02 (halves and quarters in measurement) as half-past uses the same fraction concept applied to clock time.

name: Reading and showing time to the quarter-hour
description: Students read and show quarter-past and quarter-to times, connecting the position of the minute hand to a quarter of the clock face.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown quarter-past 2, the student says the minute hand is on 3 which is a quarter of the way around, so it is quarter-past 2. For quarter-to 6, the student correctly positions the minute hand on 9.
commonError: Student can read quarter-past by recognising the minute hand on 3, but cannot read quarter-to because they do not understand the clock is three-quarters of the way around.
checkpointTask: What time is this? Now show me quarter-to 8 on the clock.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2M02 (halves and quarters) as quarter-past and quarter-to use the same fraction concept.

name: Connecting analog time to digital time notation
description: Students match analog clock displays showing hour, half-hour and quarter-hour times to the corresponding digital notation.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown an analog clock at half-past 9, the student writes 9:30 and explains that 30 means 30 minutes past the hour which is the same as half-past.
commonError: Student writes the hour correctly but writes :50 or :15 for half-past without connecting half to 30 minutes.
checkpointTask: Match each clock face to the correct digital time. Write the digital time for this analog clock.

name: Reading and setting time in everyday contexts
description: Students read times from analog clocks in familiar situations (school timetable, daily routine) and use this to sequence events.
exampleOfSuccess: Looking at the class timetable showing analog clocks, the student correctly reads the start time for each lesson and puts the lessons in chronological order.
commonError: Student reads individual times correctly in isolation but cannot sequence them accurately when they are displayed out of order.
checkpointTask: Here is our class timetable with clock faces. Put the lessons in the order they happen. What time does each one start?

name: Identifying and demonstrating full and half turns
description: Students physically demonstrate a full turn (360 degrees) and a half turn (180 degrees), recognising that a half turn faces them in the opposite direction.
exampleOfSuccess: The student stands and makes a full turn back to face the same direction, then a half turn and says I am now facing the opposite way - I can see the back wall instead of the front.
commonError: Student makes an approximate turn without checking whether they have returned to the start (full) or reversed direction (half).
checkpointTask: Stand up. Show me a full turn. Now show me a half turn. Where are you facing now?

name: Identifying and demonstrating quarter turns
description: Students physically demonstrate a quarter turn left and right, recognising that four quarter turns complete a full rotation.
exampleOfSuccess: The student makes a quarter turn right, names the new direction they are facing, and confirms that four quarter turns in the same direction bring them back to the start.
commonError: Student confuses quarter turn with half turn, rotating too far or not far enough.
checkpointTask: Show me a quarter turn to the right. What are you facing now? How many quarter turns make a full turn?

name: Identifying and demonstrating three-quarter turns
description: Students demonstrate a three-quarter turn and connect it to three quarter turns in the same direction, or equivalently one quarter turn in the opposite direction.
exampleOfSuccess: The student makes a three-quarter turn clockwise and then shows that a quarter turn anticlockwise from the same start arrives at the same position, saying going three-quarters one way is the same as going a quarter the other way.
commonError: Student makes a three-quarter turn by doing a half then estimating an additional quarter, without understanding the relationship to quarter turns.
checkpointTask: Show me a three-quarter turn. Is there a shorter way to get to the same position?

name: Giving and following turning directions in movement activities
description: Students give and follow instructions that include quarter, half and three-quarter turns to move themselves or objects through a space.
exampleOfSuccess: The student successfully navigates a partner through a simple obstacle course using instructions like forward 3 steps, quarter turn right, forward 2 steps, half turn.
commonError: Student uses turn instructions that are approximately correct but does not distinguish between quarter and half turns, causing navigation errors.
checkpointTask: Guide your partner through this obstacle course using turning instructions. They must not look!

name: Connecting turns to clock hand movement
description: Students relate quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns to the movement of clock hands, using this to reinforce both concepts.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says the minute hand makes a quarter turn from 12 to 3, a half turn from 12 to 6, a three-quarter turn from 12 to 9, and a full turn in one hour.
commonError: Student understands turns in body movement contexts but does not connect them to the rotational movement of clock hands.
checkpointTask: Watch the minute hand. From 12 to 3 - is that a quarter turn or a half turn? How do you know?
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2M04 (reading analog clock) as turns and clock hand movement are the same rotational concept.

name: Identifying turns in everyday objects and the environment
description: Students identify quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns in the movement of everyday objects such as door handles, taps, wheels and dials.
exampleOfSuccess: The student observes a tap being turned and says that is a quarter turn to open it a little, and a half turn to open it fully, making the connection between everyday action and the mathematical concept.
commonError: Student can demonstrate turns with their body but does not transfer the concept to the movement of objects, treating object rotation as a different kind of action.
checkpointTask: Watch me turn this tap. Is that a quarter turn, half turn or full turn? Where else do you see turns like this?
